title: Clinical Informatics of Xerostomia: Characterizing Comorbidities, Social Risk Factors, and Predicting Oral Health Outcomes Using Structured and Unstructured EHR Data
text:
Xerostomia (dry mouth) is a common condition with serious oral health problems and reduced quality of life. This
project will apply clinical informatics methods to develop a model to predict the risk of oral health complications.
The findings will support strategies for personalized prevention and treatment planning.

title: Multiplex single-cell chemical genomics to identify small molecule modulators of tumor cell-intrinsic immunogenicity in glioblastoma
text:
The prognosis of glioblastoma, the most aggressive primary brain cancer, remains largely unchanged in the last
two decades. Cancer immunotherapy strategies have emerged as viable treatment strategies for various
aggressive solid tumors but have met low patient response rates in glioblastoma. The proposed research aims
to leverage a novel phenotype-based single-cell transcriptomic screen to identify small molecules that alter the
ability of the immune system to target glioblastoma cells for destruction and help fulfill the promise of cancer
immunotherapy for this devastating disease.

title: Cardiac Ultrasound Radiomics-Guided Deep Neural Networks for Acute Myocardial Infarction Precision Phenotyping
text:
In the US, a heart attack occurs every 40 seconds and over 25% die within the first year after hospitalization. By
conducting this study, we will use artificial intelligence techniques to develop a software that can automatically
extract quantitative imaging features from the ultrasound images of the heart to identify patients with heart attack
who are at high-risk of death or developing complications. This will help doctors and hospitals to develop high-
precision decision-support tools for early identification and referral of high-risk patients for individualized care at
cardiac specialty clinics.

title: A novel method to identify regulators of biological aging  based on high-throughput sequencing of epigenetic clocks.
text:
Developing accurate, cost-effective, and scalable biomarkers of aging and age-related frailty could help in
assessing longevity interventions in the lab or patient outcomes in the context of clinical trials of age-related
disease. This proposal describes the development of a method for high-throughput assay of DNA methylation
clocks, a robust class of age predictors, which will be used to make a novel type of biomarker based on age and
mouse frailty scores. Additionally, this research will probe the mechanistic underpinnings of DNA methylation
clocks and epigenomic change with age in mouse muscle using the novel method for clock analysis in
combination with established genomic techniques.

title: Translational Biology Core
text:
(Core B) 
Core B, the Translational Biology core of this program project, provides support to the projects for the execution 
of common methods including animal radiotherapy and histopathological analysis maintenance and for 
standardization of cell lines and shared resources. It is also responsible for development of improved methods 
for target identification and treatment planning to improve the accuracy and reproducibility of small animal 
irradiation. These are essential services that are common to all projects.

title: Systems Biology Core
text: The overall goal of the Systems Biology Core (Core C) is to provide computational genomics and machine learning (ML) modeling expertise to the 3 projects in the P50. This expertise will utilize high dimensional datasets generated by the research projects including scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq and proteomics. These datasets will be leveraged using a suite of computational tools, either individually or in an integrated manner to address major biological questions posed by the research projects. Thus, the Core C team will function as an essential collaborative group that will help to test hypotheses and to generate predictions as well as causal inferences underlying the pathophysiology of distinct manifestations of SSc (Project 1) including SSc-ILD (Project 2) and SSc-PAH (Project 3). The aims of Core C include the inference of cell-intrinsic TF-directed genomic programs and cell-extrinsic, intercellular signaling pathways underlying SSc cellular states as well as the identification of gene/protein and module-centric predictive biomarkers of SSc outcomes. These will be enabled via a wide range of state-of-the- art computational genomics and machine learning approaches. Overall, Core C is strongly integrated with the key biological objectives of all 3 projects.

title: Modeling and targeting tumor-immune signaling interactions in tumor microenvironment
text:
Tumor-stroma/immune cell signaling communications within tumor microenvironment (TME) play important
roles in tumor development and responses to targeted and immunotherapies; whereas, the complex and
essential signaling communications within TME remain mysteries. Herein, we aim to develop novel systems
biology models, combining cutting edge technologies, i.e., artificial intelligence (AI) models, pooled-library
crispr, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), and 3D scalable tumor-stroma/immune cell co-culture assays
(tumor-on-a-chip), and state-of-the-art cancer genetic mouse models to uncover novel tumor-stroma/immune
cell signaling communications. And, we will identify novel therapeutic targets, drugs/drug combinations,
inhibiting the tumor-stroma/immune signaling communications, to improve treatment response of targeted and
immunotherapies.

title: Genetic mapping of the inflammatory adaption circuit in epithelial stem cells
text:
A remarkable feature of epithelial stem cells is their ability to rapidly detect, respond, and endure
environmental perturbations. This project aims to develop an integrative genetic platform to investigate
how epithelial stem cells sense and adapt to inflammation by modulating immune cells to rebuild a new
niche and by reprograming their metabolism to reduce inflammatory damage. The goal of this project is
to understand how these adaptive functions of epithelial stem cells promote successful wound repair.

title: Identifying roles for mitochondria and small molecules in stomata lineage asymmetrical cell division and stem cell fate regulation
text:
Stem cell division and fate determination are critical in development and play an important role in many human
diseases. This proposed research will reveal how mitochondria and associated small molecules regulate stem
cell proliferation and fate commitment in the model species Arabidopsis thaliana. Elucidating cellular and
metabolic mechanisms regulating stem cell behavior in an evolutionarily divergent species will reveal deeply
conserved mechanisms controlling tissue patterning.

title: A novel cartridge-based sequencing solution for decentralized M. tuberculosis resistance detection
text:
Our overall goal is to improve patient outcomes through the development and evaluation of simplified
sequencing workflows in order to facilitate early, appropriate drug-resistant tuberculosis treatment within
national tuberculosis programs, and to preserve newer all oral treatment regimens.

title: Diabetes Research Center (DRC)
text:
The UCSD/UCLA DRC will enhance research into the etiology, pathophysiology, treatment, and prevention of
diabetes and its complications through facilitation of scientific exchange, and advancement of the outstanding
scientific faculty comprising our research base, by providing access to novel biomedical research cores and
promoting the careers of young scientists. This will ultimately improve the lives of patients with diabetes, who
will benefit from the advancements the center will generate.

title: DEFINING REGULATORY ROLES FOR HISTONE H3 METHYLATION IN DEVELOPMENT
text:
In principle, stem cells can be directed to produce desired cell types for transplantation, disease modeling, and
drug testing, which is the basis for their tremendous scientific and therapeutic potential. However, we have not
yet realized this potential because we do not fully understand the regulatory mechanisms that maintain stem
cells and instruct their differentiation. The research outlined in this proposal will define the regulatory role of
methylation at two key histone residues, H3K9 and H3K36, in directing differentiation, both in vitro and in vivo.

title: Assimilating high-resolution behavioral and neural data across heterogeneous experimental configurations
text:
RELEVANCE
We will develop a new computational platform enabling investigation of neural representations of complex natural
behaviors over multiple modalities, brain regions, and species. Our innovative technology will provide a flexible,
centralized platform for compiling and relating neurobehavioral observations across labs and drive discovery of
how sensation and action are encoded and controlled by the nervous system, including how these neural
systems go awry in disease. The technological leap made possible by this grant will catalyze a host of studies
on the neural mechanisms underlying motor control, social behavior, learning, and neuropsychiatric disorders,
thus advancing new diagnostic and therapeutic approaches for patients.

title: Mechanisms of Mu Opioid Receptor Trafficking and Signaling at Primary Cilia
text:
Mu opioid receptors (MORs), key targets for pain relief, also carry high risk for addiction and overdose. Recent
evidence shows MORs signal from multiple cellular compartments, suggesting that their location may influence
function. This proposal investigates how MORs are regulated and function at neuronal primary cilia using
molecular tools, proteomics, and electrophysiology to uncover mechanisms of spatially restricted opioid
signaling.

title: Spectral Cherenkov Imaging for Quantitative Dosimetry and Physiological Monitoring of Radiation Therapy
text:
Cherenkov imaging captures the low light signal generated within tissue during electron or photon therapy,
offering potential as a non-invasive, 2D, real-time tool for surface dosimetry. However, the emissive nature of
Cherenkov light leads to unpredictable spectral attenuation by superficial tissue which distorts the immediate
relationship between intensity and dose, and although these tissue properties create characteristic traits in the
emission signal, spectral analysis has yet to be utilized to enhance data quality and restore this relationship. This
research aims to develop, test, and clinically translate the technique of spectral Cherenkov imaging, transforming
it into a robust real time dosimetry tool that enables inter-fractional monitoring of physiological development in
response to therapy and leads to more informed treatment with potential for improved clinical outcomes.

title: Structural Insights into Transient States in HIV-1 Broadly Neutralizing Antibody Interactions
text:
The development of an effective HIV-1 vaccine remains a critical global health challenge due to
the virus's exceptional genetic diversity and immune evasion strategies. Broadly neutralizing
antibodies (bnAbs), which can neutralize diverse strains of HIV-1, provide a template for vaccine
development. This proposal aims to uncover the structure of the transition state that brings
these antibodies together with their target HIV-1 antigen and to design immunogens using
advanced artificial intelligence models.

title: Live Imaging and Functional Evaluation Core
text: PROJECT SUMMARY – LIVE IMAGING AND FUNCTIONAL EVALUATION (LIFE) CORE Central to understanding and treating vision loss, a major goal of the National Eye Institute (NEI), is imaging changes in the structure of the eye and retina as well as functionally evaluating vision in animal models of eye diseases. The LIFE Core provides these critical services to the NEI funded investigators at the Jules Stein Eye Institute and the broader UCLA community. The Core allows imaging the eyes and retinas of small animals using optical coherence tomography (OCT) techniques and fundoscopy. These approaches allow for imaging the cornea, anterior segment, and retina. The Core also provides services to perform in vivo electroretinography (ERGs) and visually evoked potentials (VEPs), two non-invasive approaches for measuring the function of the retina and visual system. Finally, the Core provides services for running animal behaviors, such as measuring the optokinetic reflex and cricket hunting. All of these services can be run by a staff technician, or the staff technician can train members of NEI-funded laboratories at UCLA to perform the above measurements. These approaches allow the structure and function of the visual system to be measured in living animals, which allows tracking deterioration of the visual system in disease models and determining the therapeutic potential of diverse treatments for vision-related diseases. These capabilities expand and amplify the research of NEI-funded investigators accelerating research to prevent and treat vision loss.

title: The role of genetic and epigenetic variation in the progression of IDH mutant gliomas
text:
The proposed research will identify the drivers that promote the progression of IDH mutant
gliomas and provide candidate therapeutic targets for slowing down this process.

title: Mechanisms of Muscle Wasting in ARDS: The Role of IL-6 and Mononuclear Phagocytes
text:
Acute severe respiratory failure can lead to profound, chronic muscle weakness, and there are no available
treatments to target the underlying mechanisms. We propose to investigate the role of the inflammatory cytokine,
interleukin-6, in driving early muscle wasting and evaluate whether blocking monocyte and macrophage
activation, key sources of interleukin-6, can mitigate this effect. This work will advance understanding of immune-
mediated muscle injury in acute respiratory distress syndrome and lay the groundwork for novel therapeutic
strategies.

title: Bioinformatics and Computational Biology Core (BCB)
text: PROJECT ABSTRACT/SUMMARY Bioinformatics and Computational Biology Core (BCB) Alzheimer's disease (AD) affects about 40 million people worldwide today and is the most common form of dementia found predominantly in the elderly. AD is a highly heterogeneous disease with major symptoms including progressive memory and cognitive domain deterioration over years, which eventually leads to death about 3-9 years after diagnosis. During the past few decades, many hypotheses have been proposed as potential mechanisms for AD, which involve multiple biological processes such as proteopathogenesis, mitochondrial abnormality, viral infection, and other glia cell-mediated immunological responses. However, the disease etiology and mechanism still remain unclear, and currently, there is still no curative treatment for AD. During the past years, multiple endeavors have been taken by the AD research community to identify potential drug targets and large amount of data have been generated which enables mining for evidences for drug targets. The large amount of data accumulated from these projects calls for deeper analysis coupled with extensive downstream drug development technologies to refine the target candidate lists and also identify potential new targets as well as possible drugs. As part of the Indiana University School of Medicine Purdue University TaRget Enablement to Accelerate Therapy Development for Alzheimer's Disease (IUSM-Purdue TREAT-AD) Center, the Bioinformatics and Computational Biology Core (BCB Core) will play a critical role. Specifically, the BCB Core will continue to develop advanced and novel data integration methods for predicting and prioritizing drug targets. These targets will be further refined based on additional evidences from data and experiments in collaboration with other cores of the IUSM-Purdue TREAT-AD Center. In addition, the BCB core will leverage the recent development of AI technology to develop an AI-based pipeline for predicting small molecules targeting specific proteins. The pipeline is based on advanced graph-learning methods developed by the team and will initially focus on specific protein kinases. Last but not the least, the BCB Core will provide biostatistics design and bioinformatics data analysis support for the entire center covering the lifecycle of the AD drug target identification and testing by closely collaborating and coordinating with other cores for the TREAT-AD Center. The BCB core will maintain frequent interactions with the rest of the center and also actively communicate the other Center in the TREAT-AD consortium for data standards, tool sharing, and best practices.
